## `nvs telemetry show` prints the exact payload the next upload would send, and the schema, the endpoint contracts and the aggregated data are all published

`rule:tooling/telemetry-show-prints-the-payload`

`nvs telemetry show` prints the exact payload the next upload would send, before anything is sent, and its
bytes equal what the listener then receives. That is what makes the design falsifiable rather than
promised: a reader can compare the printed payload against the closed counter schema
([`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set)) with no trust in prose.

The client side is published when this ships. The reference's tools chapter documents both consents,
the complete counter list and both endpoints' contracts, and that chapter is the user-facing statement
of what is collected. The service side is `apps/telemetry/`
([`tooling/the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program)): it keeps weekly totals only
([`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only)), stores no address
([`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address)), and publishes every total
([`tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public)), so anyone can see exactly what the project sees.

`show` prints the payload alone on standard output, so it can be compared byte for byte. It prints the
`pending` week when there is one, and otherwise the current week as it stands, with a note on standard
error that the week is not finished. With nothing recorded it prints nothing, and says so on standard
error. The upload sends the same function's bytes, and a test holds the bytes a listener on loopback
receives equal to what `show` printed just before.

<sub>See also [`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set), [`tooling/telemetry-is-two-opt-ins`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-is-two-opt-ins), [`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-serving-process-never-uploads"></a>

## An upload carries only the previous finished week, rides a short-lived user-initiated command at most weekly, and a process that has bound a socket never uploads

`rule:tooling/a-serving-process-never-uploads`

Only the **previous, finished week's** aggregate is ever sent — never a live stream — at most once a week,
at a randomized point inside the eligible window. An empty week is not sent, a week bucket in the future is
never sent, and a second upload inside the same week is refused locally.

The upload is carried by the next short-lived, user-initiated invocation that notices "telemetry is on and
a finished week is unsent". `nvs update-check` is the natural carrier — an ops team cronning it on
production boxes is exactly the short-lived process this rule wants — and `nvs telemetry upload` exists
for schedulers that want only that. There is no daemon, no timer and no background process.

**A process that has bound a socket records and never uploads.** The auditable claim is one sentence:
`nvs serve` makes zero outbound telemetry connections, under load, while still incrementing
`invocation.serve`. Every claim here is testable against a local listener, because the endpoint is
configuration ([`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration)).

**The carriers are an allow-list.** `carries_upload` in `crates/nvs-cli/src/main.rs` is one `match`
that names every command, and only `update-check` and `telemetry upload` answer yes. A new command
does not compile until it answers, so an allow-list fails closed. The answer reaches the telemetry
module once, at startup, and a process it said no for sends nothing whatever it calls. A service's
stored line answers no. `crates/nvs-cli/tests/telemetry.rs` runs `nvs serve` with a finished week
waiting and the upload URL at a listener, and the listener accepts no connection.

**The window.** A finished week's point is the Monday 00:00 UTC that ends it plus a random offset
under 24 hours, drawn the first time a carrier sees the week and kept in the counter file as `due`
([`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set)). A carrier that runs before the point sends
nothing and prints `telemetry: week <week> is sent from <time>`. The point is never inside the ISO
week of the last accepted upload. An accepted week leaves the file, so `nvs telemetry upload` with
nothing waiting prints `telemetry: no finished week is waiting to be sent`.

**Declined:**
- **A background daemon or timer that phones home.** It is the shape people distrust even when opted
  in, and a second long-lived process to secure. An upload is carried, never initiated by a resident
  process.
- **Uploading from the serving process, even once at startup.** It breaks the one-sentence claim above.

<sub>See also [`tooling/telemetry-is-two-opt-ins`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-is-two-opt-ins), [`tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`](tooling.md#tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command), [`tooling/update-check-states-the-whole-picture`](tooling.md#tooling-update-check-states-the-whole-picture), [`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration), [`http-server/two-deployments-and-nothing-a-proxy-owns`](http-server.md#http-server-two-deployments-and-nothing-a-proxy-owns).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command"></a>

## An upload gets three seconds, is abandoned with its counters kept when that expires or the collector asks to retry, is dropped when the collector refuses it, says so, and never changes the carrying command's exit status

`rule:tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`

An upload has a **three-second budget** end to end. When it expires, or the connection fails, the attempt
is abandoned, the counters are kept for the next carrier, and the output says exactly that —
`telemetry: could not send (timeout after 3s); kept for next time`. The carrying command's own work and
exit status are untouched, and there is no retry inside the same invocation.

The collector's answer decides what happens to the week's report
([`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema)). A `429` or a `5xx` keeps it,
the same as a timeout. A `400`, `413` or `415` drops it, because the same bytes would be refused again,
and the line says so: `telemetry: refused by the collector (400: week); dropped`. Any other status is
treated as a `5xx`.

An operator who opted in is lending a command they ran for another reason
([`tooling/a-serving-process-never-uploads`](tooling.md#tooling-a-serving-process-never-uploads)); an unreachable endpoint may cost them three seconds and
one honest line, never a failed cron job or a changed exit code
([`tooling/update-check-states-the-whole-picture`](tooling.md#tooling-update-check-states-the-whole-picture)).

**The lines.** An accepted week prints `telemetry: sent week <week>, <n> bytes` and adds to the
lifetime totals. A kept one prints `telemetry: could not send (<why>); kept for next time`, where
`<why>` is `timeout after 3s`, the transport's error, or `the collector returned <status>`. A dropped
one names the reply's first line as the field, printable ASCII only and at most 64 characters, so a
collector cannot write control characters to the terminal. The upload is one `POST` that follows no
redirect, so the body goes only to the URL that was named.

<sub>See also [`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema), [`tooling/a-serving-process-never-uploads`](tooling.md#tooling-a-serving-process-never-uploads), [`tooling/update-check-states-the-whole-picture`](tooling.md#tooling-update-check-states-the-whole-picture).</sub>

<a id="tooling-update-check-states-the-whole-picture"></a>

## `nvs update-check` always reports the telemetry switch, the local and latest versions, and with telemetry on its upload history; `--json` is stable and the exit status is always 0

`rule:tooling/update-check-states-the-whole-picture`

`nvs update-check`'s output always carries whether telemetry is on or off, the local version and the
latest released version. With telemetry on it adds when the last upload happened, when the next one is
eligible, and the lifetime totals — how many uploads, how many bytes sent — both maintained locally and
never themselves uploaded.

`--json` emits one JSON document with stable, schema-versioned field names for the user's own automation.
The default human output **streams** as it works, one line per step, so the user sees exactly where it is
when something is slow, and follows the terminal's conventions. The exit status is 0 whether or not an
update exists and whether or not a telemetry send succeeded
([`tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`](tooling.md#tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command)); automation reads the JSON.

**The human output** is these lines, in this order, each written and flushed as it happens:
`telemetry: on, ...` or `telemetry: off, ...` with the upload URL or the note that `NVS_TELEMETRY_URL`
is not set, `this
version: <v>`, `reading the latest release from <url>`, then either `latest version: <v>` and one of
`an update is available: <local> to <latest>` or `you have the latest version`, or `could not read the
latest release: <why>`. The latest version is the Releases API document's `tag_name` with a leading
`v` removed. A tag that is not 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `+` fails the read, and
the line's reason says the reply's `tag_name` is not a version, so a reply never writes another byte
to the terminal. Versions compare number by number, and a release follows its own pre-release.

**`--json`** prints `{"schema":1,"telemetry":"on"|"off","telemetry_url":…,"local":…,"latest":…,
"update_available":…,"error":…}` in that key order. `latest` and `update_available` are `null` when the
request failed, and `error` is `null` when it did not. The request is one `GET` with a ten-second
bound over the transport `Core\Http\Client` uses, and its reply is capped at 1 MiB.

The switch is on when the data folder's consent is `on` and neither `DO_NOT_TRACK` nor `CI` is set
([`tooling/telemetry-is-two-opt-ins`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-is-two-opt-ins)).

**With telemetry on**, the command carries the upload once the release is read
([`tooling/a-serving-process-never-uploads`](tooling.md#tooling-a-serving-process-never-uploads)). After the release lines it prints the upload's one
line when an upload URL is set, then `last upload: <time>` or `last upload: never`, `next upload: from
<time>` and `uploads accepted: <n>, bytes sent: <b>`. A time is UTC, as `2026-10-26T05:12:00Z`.
`--json` adds `"upload":{"result":…,"message":…}`, where `result` is `sent`, `kept`, `dropped`,
`not-due` or `nothing` and `message` is that line, then `"last_upload"`, `"next_upload"`, `"uploads"`
and `"bytes_sent"`, after `error` and in that order. Each is `null` while telemetry is off, and
`upload` is also `null` when no upload URL is set.

<sub>See also [`tooling/telemetry-is-two-opt-ins`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-is-two-opt-ins), [`tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`](tooling.md#tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command), [`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration), [`tooling/terminal-output-is-a-sink`](tooling.md#tooling-terminal-output-is-a-sink).</sub>

<a id="tooling-the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program"></a>

## The telemetry collector is `apps/telemetry/`, a Novis program in this repository that names no host, and it runs and is tested end to end on one machine

`rule:tooling/the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program`

The service that receives telemetry is `apps/telemetry/`, a Novis web application in this repository,
in the shape of `apps/notes/`. **The program names no host.** Every link and every endpoint it prints
is built from the request's own scheme and host, so the same code answers on `127.0.0.1:8000` and on
any domain. The domain is deployment configuration: the TLS proxy's site name, and the client's
`NVS_TELEMETRY_URL` ([`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration)). The client's
default URL stays empty until a collector is deployed, and setting it then is one constant in
`crates/nvs-cli/src/endpoints.rs`. It does four things and nothing else:
it checks a report ([`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema)), adds it to
the weekly totals ([`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only)), keeps every address off disk
([`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address)), and publishes all it has
([`tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public)).

The code is public because the repository is. The site's footer names the commit it was deployed
from, linked to that commit's tree, so a reader can read the exact code that answered. The deploy guide
in `apps/telemetry/README.md` is the whole deployment: the `nvs.toml`, the TLS proxy's configuration
with no log, and how the commit is recorded. Nothing about the deployment is private except the host's
own credentials.

**The whole service runs and is tested on one machine.** An end-to-end test starts `nvs serve` on the
application with a temporary database on loopback, points the real client at it through
`NVS_TELEMETRY_URL`, uploads a finished week with `nvs telemetry upload`, and reads the result back
from `/data/totals.json` and the pages. No test and no check reaches a real host. It is the one
test of the app under `nvs serve`. With no `[capabilities.fs] read`, `nvs test` reads any file and a
request reads only `public/`, so the app's `read` names `known.toml` and `REVISION`, the two files
outside `public/` it reads, and this test fails on a read the list leaves out.

The collector is a Novis program because it is small, its job is a web request, and running it is a
real-world test of the language under traffic it does not control. It shares no code, database or
process with the registry, so a fault in one never reaches the other.

- **Memory:** per request, one report of at most 4 KiB and one transaction. The rate limit's table is
  per process ([`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address)).

**Declined:**
- **A hosted analytics product or a third-party collector.** It moves the promise to a company whose
  code nobody here can read, and adds a second party to every report.
- **A separate repository.** The known command list must follow the binary's command table, and a
  test can check that only when both are in one tree.
- **Sharing the registry's process or database.** Two services with one fault domain, for no gain.
- **A domain written into the program or its `nvs.toml`.** The program would then answer correctly on
  one host only, and a local run would print links to a site that is not the one answering.

<sub>See also [`config/telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration`](config.md#config-telemetry-and-update-endpoints-are-configuration), [`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema), [`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only), [`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address), [`tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public), [`packaging/the-registry-is-a-novis-program`](packaging.md#packaging-the-registry-is-a-novis-program).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema"></a>

## `POST /v1/report` accepts one JSON report of at most 4 KiB that matches the closed schema, and refuses anything else with a status the client acts on

`rule:tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`

`POST /v1/report` takes one `application/json` body of at most 4 KiB, the exact bytes `nvs telemetry
show` printed ([`tooling/telemetry-show-prints-the-payload`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-show-prints-the-payload)), in the shape
[`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set) gives. The request carries no cookie, no token and
no identifier, and the answer sets none.

The collector checks every field, and one wrong field refuses the whole report:

| Field | Accepted |
|---|---|
| `schema` | `1` |
| `version` | `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional `-` pre-release of `[0-9a-z.]`, at most 32 bytes |
| `os`, `arch` | a value from `apps/telemetry/known.toml` |
| `week` | `YYYY-Www`, a week that ended by the collector's clock, with one day of tolerance, and is at most four weeks old |
| `first` | `true` or `false` |
| `days_active` | an integer from 1 to 7 |
| `counters` | at most 64 keys, each `invocation.<name>` or `internal-error.<name>` with `<name>` matching `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}`, each value an integer from 0 up |

A key that matches the grammar but names a command `known.toml` does not list is counted as
`invocation.unknown` or `internal-error.unknown`. So a made-up name never reaches the public pages,
and a report from a newer `nvs` still counts. A value above 100 000 is counted as 100 000: a large
honest week is kept, and one report cannot move a total by more than that. A test in the repository
checks that `known.toml` lists every command in the binary's table, so the list cannot fall behind.

The collector's clock is Core's: the week window and the rate limit's daily salt read
`Core\Time::now()`, never SQLite's `now`. So a test sets the date with `#[Test(at: ...)]` and moves it
with `Core\Test::advance` ([`testing/determinism-declared-on-the-test`](testing.md#testing-determinism-declared-on-the-test)).

The answers, and what the client does with each
([`tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`](tooling.md#tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command)):

| Status | Meaning | The client |
|---|---|---|
| `204` | added to the totals | records the upload |
| `400` | a field is wrong; the body names it | drops that week's report |
| `413` | the body is over 4 KiB | drops that week's report |
| `415` | not `application/json` | drops that week's report |
| `429` | the address sent too many reports; `Retry-After` says when | keeps it for next time |
| `5xx` | the collector failed | keeps it for next time |

A report the client sent twice, because its three-second budget ran out after the collector had
already answered `204`, is counted twice. That case is rare, the cost is one report, and preventing it
needs an identifier on every report.

**Declined:**
- **Refusing a report over a value cap.** It loses an honest heavy week, and the cap already bounds
  what one report can move.
- **A signed report or a per-install key.** A key is an identifier, and the anonymity is worth more
  than the spam it would stop. The rate limit and the caps bound the damage
  ([`tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address)).
- **Accepting any version string.** A free-text field would put whatever a sender writes on a public
  page.

<sub>See also [`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set), [`tooling/a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command`](tooling.md#tooling-a-failed-upload-never-fails-the-command), [`tooling/the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program), [`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only).</sub>

<a id="tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only"></a>

## The collector adds each report to weekly totals per version, os and arch in one transaction, and never stores the report itself

`rule:tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`

The collector adds an accepted report to running totals in one SQLite transaction, and the report is
never written anywhere: not to a table, a file, a queue or a log. Each total is keyed on the report's
`week`, `version`, `os` and `arch`, and there are two tables:

| Table | One row per | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| `reports` | week, version, os, arch | `reports`, `first_reports`, and `active_1` to `active_7`: how many reports had each `days_active` |
| `counters` | week, version, os, arch, counter | `total`, the sum of the counter's values, and `reports`, how many reports had it above zero |

`reports` is how many installs sent a report that week, because an install sends at most one per week.
A counter's `reports` is how many of those installs used the command. That is usually the question,
and its `total` alone is easily skewed by one install that ran the command in a loop.

A row that only one report made is still anonymous: the report carries no identifier, no address and
nothing a person typed, so the row says only that one install of that version on that system ran
those commands that week. The totals are kept for as long as the service runs, and every one of them
is public ([`tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public)). So the project sees exactly what everybody
sees.

- **Memory:** one transaction per request. The database grows by at most one row per week, version,
  system and counter, which is bounded by the closed lists and not by the number of reports.

**Declined:**
- **Storing raw reports and computing totals later.** A raw report is one install's week. Not
  storing it is the simplest way to make sure nobody, including the project, can ever look at one.
- **Separate one-field tables, with no week by version by system cross-table.** It answers fewer
  questions, and the cross-table reveals nothing about a person, because a report carries nothing
  about one.
- **Deleting old weeks.** The totals are anonymous and public already, and history is what makes them
  useful.

<sub>See also [`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema), [`tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public), [`tooling/telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-counters-are-a-closed-set).</sub>

<a id="tooling-the-collector-never-stores-an-address"></a>

## The collector never stores a sender's address: it limits the rate on a keyed hash held in memory, and its server and proxy write no address to any log

`rule:tooling/the-collector-never-stores-an-address`

No sender's address is written to disk, by the program, the Novis server or the TLS proxy in front of
it. The address lives in memory for one request, and once more as a keyed hash in the rate limit.

- **The rate limit.** Each report calls `Core\RateLimit::shed` with ten reports per hour per address,
  before the report is read (`apps/telemetry/src/Limit.nvs`). The key is a SHA-256 of a 32-byte salt
  from `Core\Random` followed by the address. The salt is kept in `Core\Cache::memory()` under the
  UTC date and expires at the end of that day, so a key cannot be linked across days and nothing
  reverses it. Two cores that start a day at the same moment can each make a salt, and the later one
  stays: a sender's first reports of that day may then count under two keys. `shed` keeps its count in the serving process's memory
  ([`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members)). A refused report gets `429` with `Retry-After`.
- **The server's log.** The application's `nvs.toml` sets `[log] client_ip = false`
  ([`http-server/a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address`](http-server.md#http-server-a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address)), so not even a `5xx` line carries
  the address. The program never passes the address to `Core\Log`.
- **The proxy.** The deploy guide's proxy configuration has no access log, and the Novis server
  trusts it as its one proxy, so `Core\Request::clientIp()` is the sender and not the proxy.

An office of many developers behind one address sends a few reports a week, far under the limit.
A flood from one address is cut off within the first ten reports of an hour. A flood from many
addresses is not stopped, and the value cap bounds what each report can add
([`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema)). That damage is accepted, and
an identifier that would stop it is not.

A test sends reports from a known address and then reads every table and every log line the test
server wrote, and the address is in none of them.

- **Memory:** per process, one GCRA timestamp per address that sent a report in the last hour, and
  one 32-byte salt.

`apps/telemetry/src/LimitTest.nvs` sends reports with no address through the application and gets
`429` with `Retry-After` on the eleventh. It gives `Limit` known addresses as well: an hour later the
allowance is back, a new day gives a new key, and neither the address nor its key is in either
table. `Core\Test::request` sends no address, so the log half runs in the end-to-end test against
`nvs serve`.

**Declined:**
- **`Core\Hash::hmac` under the salt.** Its key is a `secret bytes`, and `Core\Cache::memory()` gives
  a cached salt back `tainted`. Keeping it `secret` would mean sealing it with `putSecret` under a key
  ring the operator configures. A hash of the fixed-length salt and the address does the same job
  here, because nothing checks a key against a message.
- **Storing a hashed address to count unique installs.** The weekly gate already makes one report
  one install, and a stored hash with a known salt is an address list that is easy to rebuild.
- **Rate limiting in the proxy alone.** The promise would then depend on configuration nobody can
  test with the program. The limit in the program is tested with it.
- **No rate limit.** One script could then write any number into the public totals.

<sub>See also [`http-server/a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address`](http-server.md#http-server-a-log-line-can-leave-out-the-client-address), [`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members), [`tooling/the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program), [`tooling/a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema`](tooling.md#tooling-a-telemetry-report-is-checked-against-a-closed-schema).</sub>

<a id="tooling-telemetry-totals-are-public"></a>

## Every total the collector keeps is public, on server-rendered pages with no script, no cookie and no third-party request, and as JSON and CSV under CC0

`rule:tooling/telemetry-totals-are-public`

The collector publishes every total it keeps, and the project reads the same
pages and files as anyone else. There is no private view and no admin page.

| Path | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `/` | reports per week over all weeks, first reports per week, and for the last finished week: versions, systems, how many installs used each command, the `days_active` spread, and internal errors per command |
| `/collect` | what a report contains, field by field, an example, how to turn telemetry on and off, and links to the source and the deployed commit |
| `/data` | the download list and the CC0 notice |
| `/data/totals.json`, `/data/totals.csv` | both tables in full |
| `/data/<week>.json` | one week's rows |

The pages are HTML rendered on the server, and the charts are SVG in the page. A page loads no
script, sets no cookie and requests nothing from another host. Its `Content-Security-Policy` is
`default-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'`. Reports for a week arrive for up to four weeks
after it ends, so the newest four finished weeks are marked as still arriving. The text on the pages is
written to `AGENTS.md` § *Text an end user reads*.

The data is CC0: anyone may copy, chart or republish it without asking.

- **Memory:** per request, the rows of the page it renders. The pages read the totals and write nothing.

**How it is built.** The application's gate (`apps/telemetry/src/Gate.nvs`) sets the policy on every
answer, an error answer included, so the header does not depend on `[http.headers]`. The stylesheet is
`/style.css`, because the policy allows no style in the page. The week the home page details is the
newest week with rows; the collector takes a report only for a finished week, so that is the last
finished week whenever one arrived. `/data/totals.csv` is one file with a first column `table`, which
is `reports` or `counters`, and the columns of both tables; a column the row's table lacks is empty.
`/data/<week>.json` is `404` for a week with no `reports` row.

**Declined:**
- **A JavaScript chart library.** It is a script on a page that promises to run none, and SVG drawn
  on the server shows the same lines.
- **Suppressing rows that few reports made.** The project would then see more than the public, and
  a row has nothing personal in it to hide ([`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only)).

<sub>See also [`tooling/the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only`](tooling.md#tooling-the-collector-keeps-weekly-totals-only), [`tooling/telemetry-show-prints-the-payload`](tooling.md#tooling-telemetry-show-prints-the-payload), [`tooling/the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-telemetry-collector-is-a-novis-program).</sub>

<a id="tooling-the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program"></a>

## The repository's tools are one Bun + TypeScript program, `bun nv`, and `smol-toml` is its only runtime dependency

`rule:tooling/the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program`

Every tool that builds, checks, renders or drives this repository is a subcommand of one program,
`bun nv <command>`, written in TypeScript and run by Bun at the version `package.json` pins. Its one
runtime dependency is `smol-toml`, which reads the TOML files the tree still has; `Bun.TOML` is never
used, so one parser reads all of them. The dev dependencies are `typescript` and `@types/bun`, and any
other dependency is a new decision. Two parts are Rust, each a crate outside the workspace that
`bun nv` builds and runs. `tools/nv-scan` is what the check selection and the perf ledger read Rust
source with, because only a parser reads Rust exactly; its dependencies are `syn`, `proc-macro2`,
`quote` and `sha2` at the versions the workspace already locks. `tools/covwrap` is the compiler wrapper
of the `covws` build, and it has no dependencies.

This is the repository's tooling, not the language's: nothing here reaches the `nvs` binary, a Novis
program or a request. What it costs is that every developer and every CI job needs Bun, which is one
binary on Windows, macOS and Linux.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping the Python scripts.** Each script carried its own parser for a shape another script also
  parsed, and two readers of one shape drifted apart.
- **More runtime dependencies**, such as a schema or a command-line library. Each one is a
  supply-chain input to every contributor's machine, and the schema builder is a few hundred lines.
- **Reading Rust source with regular expressions over lexed text.** A wrong match there does not fail
  loudly: it gives two different programs one digest, and a check that should run is skipped.

<sub>See also [`tooling/a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record`](tooling.md#tooling-a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record), [`tooling/a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited`](tooling.md#tooling-a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record"></a>

## A fact a repository tool reads is one JSON record under `data/`, its type declared once and its text written by one writer

`rule:tooling/a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record`

A fact a repository tool reads — a goal, the chain, a rule's structure, a gap, a playbook bullet, a
plan field — is one JSON file under `data/`, holding one entity. Its type is
declared once in `tools/nv/schema/`, and that declaration is the static type, the runtime check and
the JSON Schema together. `tools/nv/lib/store.ts` is the only code that writes a record: keys in
schema order, two-space indent, LF and one trailing newline. So one value has one text, loading a
record and writing it back changes nothing, and git merges two edits to one record line by line. No
record is TOML.

An id is a slug or a number, and it never changes. A reference is an id, and `bun nv check` fails on
one that names no record.

Prose stays under `docs/` at its own path — a rule fragment, a goal's prose, a reference chapter —
so every citation into it still resolves. Where a prose file repeats a field a
record holds, the record is the authority and a check compares the copy to it. A shape that once had
a checker of its own is a schema, and `bun nv check` is the one audit of all of them.

**Declined:**
- **TOML records.** A second writer cannot reproduce a TOML file's text from its value without a
  formatting library, and JSON is what the website and the editors already read.

<sub>See also [`tooling/the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program), [`tooling/a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited`](tooling.md#tooling-a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited"></a>

## A file rendered from the records is committed, marked generated and never edited, and a conflict in one is resolved by rendering it again

`rule:tooling/a-rendered-file-is-committed-and-never-edited`

A file a tool writes from the records is committed, so GitHub and a reader without Bun see it. It
opens with a marker naming the command that writes it, and `.gitattributes` gives it
`linguist-generated`, so a review folds it away. It is never edited by hand: the change goes into the
record or the prose fragment it is rendered from, and the file is rendered again.

The command that writes it has a check form that writes nothing and fails when the file no longer
matches its sources — `bun nv render --check` for the website's pages and data, `bun nv rules --render
--check` for the rulebook's chapters and `docs/ground-rules.md`. CI's `docs` job runs both. After a
merge conflict in a rendered file, it is rendered again from the merged
records, never merged by hand. A rendered file shows in a diff beside the record change that caused it.

**Declined:**
- **Rendering on demand and committing nothing generated.** GitHub would show no rulebook, and a
  reader would need Bun to read the rules.

<sub>See also [`tooling/a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record`](tooling.md#tooling-a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record).</sub>

<a id="tooling-the-chain-names-its-live-goal"></a>

## The chain in the goals README names the live goal, and a reached goal's file is deleted with none of its checks carried

`rule:tooling/the-chain-names-its-live-goal`

The loop's live goal is the first slug of the `chain:` list in the front matter of `docs/goals/README.md`,
committed like every other file. So a fresh clone, CI and a git hook read the same live goal looper works
on, and nothing about which goal is live is kept only on the machine that ran the loop. `looper goal new`
and `looper goal move` edit the list.

A reached goal's file under `docs/goals/` is deleted, its slug leaves the chain, and the next slug is the
live goal. Nothing is archived, and `git log` is the history. A decision that only a goal's prose holds is
moved to its home before the goal is reached: a rule fragment, a module doc or a test. A reached goal kept on disk would hold nothing a later session reads, and would still be a
document that cites code and drifts from it, with every tool carrying a branch to tell it from a live
one. A regression in finished work is caught by the suite that tests it, or by nothing.

No goal's checks are carried as a floor: `looper.toml` sets `carry_to_floor = false`. A goal's plan is its
own front matter and nothing else. The permanent suites and `bun nv verify` protect finished work, and a
check that proves more than a suite becomes a test before its goal is reached.

The runtime state stays git-ignored: the selection store in `.cache/select.sqlite`, and looper's run
state under `.loop/`. It is per machine, and a fresh clone owes nothing it holds.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping the live goal in the git-ignored run state.** A fresh clone has no such file, so it has no
  live goal: the orientation and CI read nothing, and a push hook that needs the live goal refuses
  every push.
- **Carrying a reached goal's test checks into a floor, whole or reduced to one check per crate and
  per case tree.** Most of them re-run what `bun nv verify` already runs, and the floor grows with
  every goal reached. A check written for an early goal also pins that goal's view of the engine, so
  when the engine moves on a session has to edit the record of a goal it has never seen.
- **Keeping the floor and deleting only a reached goal's prose.** Its checks would still have to stay
  current against code that moves on, which is the drift deleting the goal removes.
- **Archiving reached goals under another directory.** An archive is a document nobody reads that
  still matches every search, and `git log` already holds it.

<sub>See also [`tooling/a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record`](tooling.md#tooling-a-repository-fact-is-one-json-record).</sub>

<a id="tooling-a-check-runs-only-when-the-change-reaches-its-footprint"></a>

## A check runs only when the change reaches what its green runs were observed to use, and the pipeline runs and records on the one `covws` debug build

`rule:tooling/a-check-runs-only-when-the-change-reaches-its-footprint`

The acceptance sweep, `bun nv verify`, `bun nv affected` and `bun nv proofs` start only the atoms a
change reaches, read from what each atom's green runs were observed to use. An atom is the smallest
thing that runs on its own: one `.nvst` case, one proof program, one Rust test binary, one `bun nv`
command, one tools test file, one other plan check. Every run of one records its footprint in
`.cache/select.sqlite`: the Rust items that ran, from coverage, and the `Core` classes, cards, files,
directories and paths it looked up, from the log `nvs` and the test binaries write. A configuration file
is recorded by part: its global tables, and the paths an `[[app]]` block that applies to the entry file
could be keyed on. An edit of the repository's own `nvs.toml` moves only the parts it changed, and the
test that resolves that file whole runs on every edit of it. A selection turns
the change since the recorded tree into keys and looks the atoms up under them. **A run counts the
moment each atom's run is recorded**, not when the whole run ends: the atom is stamped with the tree the
run's selection was read at, the next selection reads it against the change since that tree, and a
verdict judged and not yet recorded is kept the same way, so a run that is killed loses only the atoms
still running. The run that moves the recorded tree clears the stamps it covers. An atom that is new,
last red, owed or diverged runs too, and so does every atom when a global file changes. Nothing else
starts. A bench is judged on the release build, so `bun nv affected --run` judges only the benches the
change itself reaches, and `bun nv benches --owed` pays the owed ones before a release, where the
`proofs` job is red on a stale perf record.
`tools/nv/select/` is the one engine all four ask, `select.ts` there holds the rule and
`keys.ts` the keys, and `bun nv select --explain <atom>` says why one atom was chosen or not.

The footprint is observed rather than predicted because a prediction at crate granularity cannot tell
a function body a program runs from one it does not: an edit to one body re-ran thousands of cases,
and every narrowing of it was a claim someone had to prove and remember. An atom's footprint is the
union of its runs since its definition last changed, pruned of items that no longer exist, so a path
a run takes only sometimes is kept once it has been seen. Footprints are kept per platform, because
what an atom does differs between Windows and Linux, and `bun nv select --seed` records every
atom from nothing for a new platform or a lost store.

What coverage cannot see is closed over the reference graph `tools/nv-scan --items` reads: a const, a
static, a type or a table moves every item whose name Rust can resolve to it, which in another package
takes an import or a qualified path and in shipped code no dev-dependency, a `macro_rules!` every item
that invokes it,
a class table's changed row that row's class, and a card only what prints it. A row, a class or a `use`
whose only change is its link to a card or its import of a card type moves only what prints that card.
A doc-comment edit moves nothing. **Anything that cannot be attributed widens**: an unparseable file, an
unmapped function or an unreadable record selects more, never less.

The pipeline's one debug build is `covws` (`target/covws`, built by `tools/nv/lib/covws.ts` through
`tools/covwrap`), which instruments the workspace's own crates and nothing else. Every debug `nvs` and
test binary the sweep, verify, `bun nv try` and `bun nv reference` run is that build, handed to checks
as `NVS_BIN`; `target/debug` is what a person builds by hand. A recorded run starts with an empty compile
cache. A proof program is judged on the uninstrumented `target/proof` build and recorded in a second run
on `covws`, which is never a verdict; when the two runs end differently, the program always runs until
they agree.

The heavy checks, which build the release profile, fuzz, TSan or the database matrix, record no
coverage of their own. A release test, a bench and the database
matrix are keyed on a **twin**: the same work run again on `covws`, whose verdict counts for nothing and
whose coverage is the check's keys. The twin of a release test runs its tests with `--include-ignored`,
a bench runs once on the covws `nvs`, and the database matrix runs its SQLite leg. Each also holds a key
for what its twin cannot reach: `profile:optimized` for release code, and every file of `nvs-db` for the
server drivers. Code only Linux compiles moves `platform:elsewhere`, which the database matrix, fuzz
and TSan hold. Fuzz and TSan build inside WSL and have no twin: they are keyed on every
item and directory of the crates they build, the one predicted key left. A twin that cannot run or be
read records `*`, which every change reaches until a twin is read again. A check with `memoize = false`
is never answered from the store, and
`bun nv select --full` runs every atom that is not heavy.

A heavy check keyed on every file of every crate it builds would be reached by almost any Rust change,
so a goal that names them would pay for all of them after nearly every session; the twin is what keeps a
change that reaches none of its code from running it. A twin is paid only when its heavy check runs.

**The leak check is CI's nightly job, not the loop's.** `bun nv valgrind` runs every `examples/`
program under memcheck in the deep lane ([`testing/the-deep-lane`](testing.md#testing-the-deep-lane)), and CI's Linux jobs run every
test on Linux at each push. A run in the loop would be keyed on a goal's fixtures, and a goal that names
none would run nothing: the nightly job names its own programs. The debt run runs no heavy check.
Looper's sweep runs the heavy checks the live goal names, and a push to CI runs each one its diff
reaches ([`testing/ci-lanes`](testing.md#testing-ci-lanes)).

**The floor debt is paid once per goal, and nightly CI is the safety net.** An atom a change reached
that a run did not start is owed, and it stays selected until a run of it is green. `bun nv debt` is
the floor check `floor-debt` in `docs/goals/README.md`, with `reach: true`, so looper judges it last
and only once every stage is done and every other check is green. It runs the owed atoms, oldest
first: proof programs, cases, test binaries, tools tests and plan checks, and the red proof programs,
which `nv verify` never runs again. It pays all of them, and is red while any stays red. It leaves the benches to a release, because a goal's owed
benches alone took over an hour to pay. No session pays debt,
and nothing pays it between two sessions, so a red in an owed atom can stay unseen for up to one goal.
Nothing in the loop runs every atom whatever changed, so a selection miss shows up in CI's nightly deep
lane, which runs every job whatever changed. The hook after each session, `bun nv sweep`, reads the
newest nightly run back and writes each failed job beside looper's own reds in `.loop/last-sweep.md`.

`bun nv select --full` runs and records every atom that is not heavy, whatever changed, when a person
runs it. An atom red there that the selection since the store's tree did not pick is a selection miss:
it is printed, kept in the store until a full run finds the atom green again, and fails the run.
`bun nv select --mutate tools/data/select-mutations.json` is the proof that the keys lose nothing: it
applies one batch of breaking edits at a time, runs every atom that is not heavy against a copy of the
store named by `NV_SELECT_STORE`, requires every red atom to have been selected, and reverts the edits.

- **Memory:** nothing at run time; this is the development machine's disk, never a request's. The
  store and the coverage-map cache under `.cache/select/covmap/` are per machine and git-ignored, and
  grow with the number of atoms and builds, never with the number of runs. Each run's raw profile is
  deleted as it is read. The `covws` build takes the place of the pipeline's `target/debug`, at about
  the same size, and a selected proof program runs twice.

**Declined:**
- **Refining the static keys with finer tiers, more partitions and more exception lists.** Each
  refinement moved the over-selection somewhere else rather than removing it.
- **A static call graph read with `syn`.** Dynamic dispatch, the registry's lookup by name, JIT code
  calling Rust helpers through `no_mangle` symbols and closures passed across crates all hide the
  edges that matter, so the graph is unsound exactly where the runtime is interesting.
- **Judging proof programs on an instrumented optimized build.** Instrumentation slows an attack
  severalfold and some far more, which changes what an attack's time limit means. Recording on a
  second debug run costs no build and leaves the verdict on the uninstrumented one. A perf guard's
  margins would change meaning the same way, so no release test is recorded on an instrumented build.
- **A WSL leg and a valgrind sweep over the live goal's fixtures, paid as floor debt.** The goals'
  checks name no fixture, so both legs ran nothing while the debt run reported them as waiting. CI's
  Linux jobs run every test on Linux, and the nightly `valgrind` job names its own programs.
- **A full run in the loop every few sessions, whatever changed.** That run re-recorded
  every atom and judged every bench, and it held the loop for far longer than the debt the sessions
  between left. Paying the debt a fixed budget at a time costs each session the same bounded time. The
  local store is never re-recorded whole, so a selection miss is caught by nightly CI rather than here.

<sub>See also [`tooling/the-chain-names-its-live-goal`](tooling.md#tooling-the-chain-names-its-live-goal), [`tooling/the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program`](tooling.md#tooling-the-repository-tools-are-one-bun-program).</sub>
